```{r}
library(simpexp)
```

## What a formula may depend on

The right-hand side of a transition formula is evaluated on the
interval-expanded data. Besides the covariates of `data`, the simulator
provides the variables listed in `?time_scales`. Which of them a hazard uses
decides the probabilistic structure of the process -- nothing else does:

| variable | meaning | resulting process |
|---|---|---|
| `t` (`= tend`) | time since the origin of the process | Markov |
| `t_sojourn` | time already spent in the current state | semi-Markov |
| `t_entry` | time at which the current state was entered | neither |
| `n_visits_<state>` | visits to `<state>` so far | neither |
| `t_total_<state>` | time spent in `<state>` so far | neither |
| `n_transitions` | transitions made so far | neither |
| `interval` | index of the current interval of `cut` | -- |

There is no switch to set: writing `t_sojourn` into a formula *is* the
specification of a semi-Markov process.

## Markov: the clock never resets

```{r}
df <- data.frame(id = 1:2000)

markov <- sim_pexp_msm(
  list(
    transition("healthy", "ill",  ~ log(0.3)),
    transition("ill", "healthy",  ~ log(0.5)),
    transition("ill", "dead",     ~ log(0.05) + 0.1 * t)),
  df, cut = seq(0, 20, by = 0.1))
```

The hazard of dying while ill grows with calendar time, identically for a
subject who has just fallen ill and for one who has been ill for years.

## Semi-Markov: the clock resets on entry

```{r}
semi <- sim_pexp_msm(
  list(
    transition("healthy", "ill",  ~ log(0.3)),
    transition("ill", "healthy",  ~ log(0.5)),
    transition("ill", "dead",     ~ log(0.05) + 0.4 * t_sojourn)),
  df, cut = seq(0, 20, by = 0.1))
```

Now the risk depends on how long *this* episode of illness has lasted. The two
processes have the same transition structure and differ only in that one
variable; their sojourn-time distributions are visibly different.

```{r}
soj <- function(s) {
  e <- s[s$from == "ill", ]
  e$tstop - e$tstart
}
rbind(markov = summary(soj(markov)), `semi-Markov` = summary(soj(semi)))
```

Because the semi-Markov hazard rises steeply within an episode, long illness
episodes are cut short -- the sojourn distribution has a much lighter tail.

## Neither: history dependence

A process that looks back further than the current state is neither Markov nor
semi-Markov. The history features make that a one-line change.

```{r}
relapsing <- sim_pexp_msm(
  list(
    transition("healthy", "ill",  ~ log(0.3) + 0.25 * n_visits_ill),
    transition("ill", "healthy",  ~ log(0.5)),
    transition("ill", "dead",     ~ log(0.03) + 0.1 * t_total_ill)),
  df, cut = seq(0, 20, by = 0.1), keep_history = TRUE)
```

Each episode of illness makes the next one more likely, and the accumulated
time spent ill raises the risk of dying. `keep_history = TRUE` returns the
feature values the hazards were evaluated with, which is the ground truth of
the data-generating process:

```{r}
head(relapsing[c("id", "episode", "from", "to", "tstart", "tstop",
                 "n_visits_ill", "t_total_ill")], 8)
```

That the mechanism really bites can be read off the data: the rate of becoming
ill again, by the number of previous illness episodes.

```{r}
healthy <- relapsing[relapsing$from == "healthy", ]
healthy$k <- healthy$n_visits_ill
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sort(unique(healthy$k)), function(k) {
  d <- healthy[healthy$k == k, ]
  data.frame(n_visits_ill = k, episodes = nrow(d),
    rate = sum(d$to == "ill", na.rm = TRUE) / sum(d$tstop - d$tstart),
    implied = 0.3 * exp(0.25 * k))
}))
print(tab[tab$episodes > 30, ], digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The empirical occurrence/exposure rates track `0.3 * exp(0.25 * k)`, which is
what the formula asked for.

## Why oracle features matter

In a simulation study the interesting question is usually whether a method can
*recover* a dependence of this kind from the observed trajectories. Having the
true feature values alongside the data separates two failure modes: a model
that cannot represent the dependence, and a model that can but does not find
it. Fitting with the oracle features gives the ceiling against which a
data-driven model is measured.
